ref: Doukas, Historia byzantina, cap. III, Bekker p. 17 (CSHB 1834), passage on Bayezid
quote_orig: ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀράβων θρησκείᾳ μαθητὴς τοῦ Μωαμὲδ θερμότατος, φυλάττων τὰς ἀθέσμους αὐτοῦ ἐντολὰς ἄχρι καὶ τῆς ὑστάτης στιγμῆς, ἄγρυπνος καὶ διανυκτερεύων ἔν τε βουλαῖς καὶ μηχανουργίαις κατὰ τῶν Χριστοῦ λογικῶν προβάτων.
own_translation_en: In the religion of the Arabs he was a most zealous disciple of Muhammad, keeping his lawless commandments up to the last moment, sleepless and spending the nights in plots and schemes against Christ's rational sheep. (Team translation, literal.)
quote_latin: prae caeteris sui aevi hominibus Christianorum hostis, superstitionis Arabum observator studiosissimus; et Mohamedis impiis praeceptis adhaerens ea accuratissime observabat. noctes insomnes ducebat consilia struens dolosque nectens adversus Christi rationabiles oves.
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1834 (1834): public domain. archive.org mark CC Public Domain 1.0. Greek checked against the page image.
what_it_says: Doukas describes the Ottoman prince Bayezid as a disciple of Muhammad in the Arab religion who kept its lawless commandments and plotted against Christians.
context: Doukas is introducing Bayezid as the new Ottoman leader after the death of Murad and the murder of Lazar's family, in the opening of his Turkish narrative. The religious remark is a characterisation, not a theological argument.
limits: The epithet 'lawless' (ἀθέσμους) is Doukas' own polemical judgement. The Greek 'Μωαμέδ' is the Prophet, as the Latin 'Mohamedis' confirms; contrast Doukas' usage of 'Mahometes' for the Sultans in other chapters. Bekker's Greek and Latin are printed in parallel columns.

ref: Doukas, Historia byzantina, cap. XXXIII, Bekker p. 232 (CSHB 1834), treaty of Mehmed II with the city and Despot Constantine
quote_orig: ἐκεῖνος δὲ ὁ πρὸ τοῦ ἀντιχρίστου ἀντίχριστος, ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μου ποίμνης φθορεύς, ὁ ἐχθρὸς τοῦ σταυροῦ καὶ τῶν πιστευόντων εἰς τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ παγέντα, φιλικὸν προσωπεῖον ἐνδυθεὶς ὡς μαθητὴς τοῦ μεταμορφωθέντος εἰς ὄφιν Σατανᾶ, ἀποδέχεται τὴν πρεσβείαν καὶ γράφει νέας διαθήκας, καὶ ὀμνύει θεὸν τοῦ ψευδοπροφήτου καὶ τὸν συνώνυμον αὐτοῦ προφήτην καὶ τὰς μιαρὰς αὐτοῦ βίβλους καὶ ἀγγέλους καὶ ἀρχαγγέλους τοῦ στέργειν καὶ ἐμμένειν ἐφ᾽ ὅρου ζωῆς αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ καὶ ὁμονοίᾳ μετὰ τῆς πόλεως καὶ τοῦ δεσπότου Κωνσταντίνου.
own_translation_en: That one, the Antichrist before the Antichrist, destroyer of the flock of my Christ, enemy of the cross and of those who believe in him who was fixed on it, putting on a friendly mask as a disciple of Satan transformed into a serpent, accepts the embassy and draws up new treaties, and swears by the God of the false prophet and by his namesake prophet and by his impure books and angels and archangels to keep and abide by it all his life in love and concord with the city and with Despot Constantine. (Team translation, literal.)
quote_latin: ille vero ante Antichristum Antichristus, Christi domini mei caularum devastator, crucis et in eum qui cruci affixus est credentium hostis, amici personam indutus ut Satanae, qui in anguem se transformaverat, discipulus, legatos suscipit, nova foedera pangit, deum falsi prophetae sui et prophetam sibi cognominem impurosque eius libros iurat, angelos et archangelos testatus pacem se servaturum, et per totum vitae tempus cum urbe et despota Constantino
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1834 (1834): public domain. archive.org mark CC Public Domain 1.0. Greek checked against the page image.
keys: ἐκεῖνος δὲ ὁ πρὸ τοῦ ἀντιχρίστου ἀντίχριστος
θεὸν τοῦ ψευδοπροφήτου καὶ τὸν συνώνυμον αὐτοῦ προφήτην
what_it_says: Doukas calls Mehmed II the Antichrist's forerunner and says he swore a treaty by the God of the 'false prophet', his namesake prophet, and his 'impure books', i.e. the Muslim scriptures.
context: After Murad II's death (1451) the Byzantine envoys went to the new sultan, Mehmed, to congratulate him and renew the treaties with the city; the Latin names 'Mehemetem' in the sentence just before, which identifies 'that one' as Mehmed. The oath is reported as a fact, in Doukas' narrative of diplomacy.
limits: Doukas' rhetoric (Antichrist, Satan, serpent) is polemical and apocalyptic; the oath formula is reported, not quoted from a document. 'Impure books' (μιαρὰς βίβλους) is generic and does not name the Qur'an. The Greek is read from the page image (PDF p. 254); Latin from the same page.

ref: Doukas, Historia byzantina, cap. XXI, Bekker p. 112 (CSHB 1834), account of the 'false abbot' who taught among the Turks at Chios
quote_orig: πλανήσας δὲ τοὺς πάντας ἀγροίκους ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ δόγματι, ὑπούλως ἐπραγματεύετο καὶ τὴν τῶν Χριστιανῶν φιλίαν· ἐξέθετο γὰρ δόγμα, ὅστις τῶν Τούρκων εἴποι ὅτι Χριστιανοὶ οὐχ ὑπάρχουσι θεοσεβεῖς, οὗτος ἀσεβής ἐστι.
own_translation_en: Having led astray all the rustic people with this very doctrine, he also craftily cultivated the friendship of the Christians; for he laid down a doctrine that whoever among the Turks should say that the Christians are not God-fearing, that man is impious. (Team translation, literal.)
quote_latin: cumque in istud dogma omnes agrestes pertraxisset, subdole etiam Christianorum amicitiam petebat. edixit enim, quicunque Turcus Christianos pios esse negaret, eum impium esse.
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1834 (1834): public domain. archive.org mark CC Public Domain 1.0. Greek checked against the page image.
what_it_says: Doukas reports a Turkish dervish-leader ('the false abbot') who taught that Christians were God-fearing and that denying it was impiety, and whose followers treated Christians as envoys of God.
context: Doukas describes a movement on Chios and the Stylarion coast that preached shared property and friendship with Christians, and its leader's attempt to win over a Cretan hermit by messengers. The passage is about a Muslim sectarian leader (usually identified as Shaykh Bedreddin, a name Doukas does not give).
limits: This is a heterodox movement, not mainstream Islam; Doukas' label 'false abbot' is hostile. The identification with Bedreddin is from modern scholarship (not checked by me). Harshness is low because the point is tolerance towards Christians.

ref: Doukas, Historia byzantina, cap. XXXVI, Bekker p. 257 (CSHB 1834), polemic against Byzantine Christians who joined the Turks' religion
quote_orig: εἶδον γὰρ οἰκείοις ὄμμασι μονάστριαν καὶ τὰ θεῖα λόγια μεμυημένην οὐ μόνον κρεωφαγοῦσαν καὶ ἄμφια τῶν βαρβάρων τῷ σώματι περιφέρουσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ψευδοπροφήτῃ θυσίαν φέρουσαν καὶ τὴν ἀσέβειαν ἀναισχύντως ὁμολογοῦσαν.
own_translation_en: For I saw with my own eyes a nun, instructed in the divine words, who not only ate meat and wore the barbarians' garments on her body, but also offered sacrifice to the false prophet and shamelessly professed impiety. (Team translation, literal.)
quote_latin: monialem enim divinis scripturis eruditam non tantum carnibus vesci, barbara veste indutam ipse vidi, sed etiam Pseudoprophetae hostiam offerre, impietatemque impudenter profiteri.
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1834 (1834): public domain. archive.org mark CC Public Domain 1.0. Greek checked against the page image.
what_it_says: Doukas says he saw a nun who had abandoned Christian practice, ate meat and wore Turkish dress, and offered sacrifice to the 'false prophet' (Muhammad) and openly professed impiety.
context: This is in Doukas' attack on Greek Christians who abandoned the Orthodox sacraments during the Union controversy and went over to the Ottomans, just before the Mehmed II's siege preparations. The nun is an example of apostasy.
limits: The statement is about apostasy and Doukas' polemic against Greek Unionists, not an argument about Islamic doctrine; 'false prophet' is his insult. He says he saw it personally, which is his testimony, not corroborated here.

ref: Doukas, Historia byzantina, cap. XXXIV, Bekker p. 238 (CSHB 1834), Byzantine lament during Mehmed II's advance on the city (1453)
quote_orig: νῦν τὰ σήμαντρα τῆς φθορᾶς τοῦ ἡμετέρου γένους, νῦν αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ ἀντιχρίστου, καὶ τί γένωμεν ἢ τί ποιήσωμεν; ἀρθήτω ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν ἡ ζωὴ ἡμῶν, κύριε, καὶ μὴ ἴδοσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ τῶν δούλων σου τὴν φθορὰν τῆς πόλεως
own_translation_en: Now are the signals of the destruction of our race, now are the days of the Antichrist, and what shall we become, or what shall we do? Let our life be taken from us, Lord, and let the eyes of your servants not see the destruction of the city. (Team translation, literal.)
quote_latin: dies Antichristi advenerunt. quid de nobis statuetur? quid faciemus? vita nobis, domine, prius eripiatur, quam oculi servorum tuorum urbis eversionem videant.
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1834 (1834): public domain. archive.org mark CC Public Domain 1.0. Greek checked against the page image.
keys: ἀρθήτω ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν ἡ ζωὴ ἡμῶν
what_it_says: Doukas puts into the mouths of the Byzantines, as they hear of the siege, that the days of the Antichrist have come, which he uses for the Ottoman advance.
context: The sentence is spoken by Constantinopolitans and other Christians, after the news that Mehmed had built the fortress at the Bosporus (Boğazkesen). It is a lament, not a Muslim or doctrinal argument, and it frames Mehmed as Antichrist's precursor.
limits: This is a Christian lament and an eschatological label; it does not state what Islam teaches. Including it for theme M is a judgement. The passage contains no call to violence; it is a prayer for death before the city's fall. Greek read from the page image (PDF p. 260).

ref: Chronicon maius, Liber IV, cap. II, Bekker pp. 343-344 (CSHB 1838): Greek-Latin polemic 'Mohametes' and the Scriptures
quote_orig: Ὁ δὲ Moaus9 οὑτοσὶ πόϑεν λαβὼν τὰς μαρτυρίας ἐδές δαξε τὰ ῥήματα ἅπερ ἐδίδαξεν, ἤτοι δόγματα, καὶ ἐξέδωκε τὸν γόμον τοῖς ἸΠουσουλμώνοις; πάντως οὐκ ἀλλοϑὲν ἢ αὐτὸς δαυτοῦ ἐστὶν ὃ μαρτυρῶν περὲ αὐτοῦ· εἰς γὰρ πᾶσαν τὴν Jta» γραφὴν οὐκ ἀναφαίνεται περὶ αὐτοῦ μαρτυρία, εἰλλὰ τοὐναντίον.
own_translation_en: Now this Muhammad, from where did he take the testimonies with which he taught the words, that is the doctrines, which he taught, and issued the law to the Muslims? Surely from nowhere else than from himself is the one who testifies about him. For in all the divine scripture no testimony about him appears, but the opposite. (Team translation of the raw OCR; the Greek contains OCR errors, see limits.)
quote_latin: Mobametes iste autem undenam testimonia nactus praecepta sive dogmata docuit, quae docuit, constituitque legem Musulmanis? omnino e nullo alio nisi e semet ipso de se testimonium habuit. in tota enim sacra scriptura nullum comparet de illo testimonium, imo alia, quae ei contraria sint.
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1838 scan (archive.org): no licence field; PD by date (UNVERIFIED). Greek read from the OCR text layer only; not image-checked.
what_it_says: The author argues that Muhammad has no testimony from Scripture for his prophecy and that he testified to himself, so he cannot be a prophet sent by God.
context: Book IV of the Chronicon maius opens a long Greek-Latin polemic against Islam and the Prophet, after a passage on the Christians' and Muslims' views of the Gospel. The argument proceeds from Moses' promise of a prophet from the Hebrews to Christ's warning against false prophets.
limits: AUTHORSHIP DISPUTED: the Maius is widely regarded as a later compilation, not Sphrantzes' own text (see works.json). The Latin beside it reads 'Mobametes' (OCR). Not image-checked. The raw OCR join 'αὐτὸς' + 'dq? δαυτοῦ' is printed with the OCR fragment 'dq?' and the line number '10' omitted here; check the scan.

ref: Chronicon maius, Liber IV, cap. V, c. Bekker p. 360 (CSHB 1838): Mehmed's claim of a night journey revealed by Gabriel, with a quotation of Qur'an 17:1
quote_orig: καὶ γὰρ μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων πλασμάτων xai τεράτων ψευδῶν ἐπλάσατο καὶ τὴν παροῦσαν ἄϑεσμον ϑεωρίαν, ἔχουσαν ἐπὲ λέξεως οὕτως, ἐν τῷ κεφαλαίῳ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ. “αἶνος τῷ ποιήσαντι διελϑεῖν τὸν δοῦλον αὐτοῦ ἐν μιᾷ νυκτὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐχτηρίου τοῦ Ἐλαρώμ, 0 ἐστιν οἶκος Ϊεκκέ, μέχρε τοῦ πορρωτάτου εὐκτηρίου, ὃ ἐστιν οἶκος ἅγιος ᾿Ιερουσαλήμ, ἣν εὐλογήσαμεν. ὃ Μαχούμες ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν, μετὰ τὸ ψῶλαι αὐτὸν τὴν ὥραν αὑτοῦ, εἶπεν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ὦ ὑμεῖς ἄνϑρωποι, κατανοήσατε. χϑὲς μετὰ τὸ διαστῆναι μὲ ὑμῶν, ἢλθε πρός us ὃ Γαβριὴλ μετὰ τὴν ἐσχάτην ἑσπερινὴν Ψαλμῳδίαν, καὶ εἶπ μοι ᾿ὡ IModus9, ἐντέλλεται σοι ὃ ϑεὸς ἐπιδοσχέψοσθαι αὐτόν. ᾧ εἶπον “καὶ ποῦ αὐτὸν ἐπισκέψομαι ;᾽
own_translation_en: He fabricated, among other false fabrications and wonders, this lawless vision, which is worded as follows in the chapter of the Children of Israel: 'Praise to him who made his servant go by night from the sanctuary of Elarom, that is the house of Yekke, to the farthest sanctuary, which is the holy house of Jerusalem, which we have blessed.' Mahoumes, on one of the days, after the ... of his hour, said to the people: 'Consider: yesterday, after you left me, Gabriel came to us after the last evening psalmody and said to me, O Muhammad, God commands you to visit him. And I said, where shall I visit him?' (Team translation of the raw OCR; the Greek is garbled in places.)
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1838 scan (archive.org): no licence field; PD by date (UNVERIFIED). Greek read from the OCR text layer only; not image-checked.
keys: ἐν τῷ κεφαλαίῳ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ
αἶνος τῷ ποιήσαντι διελϑεῖν τὸν δοῦλον αὐτοῦ
what_it_says: The author says Mehmed (called Mahoumes) fabricated a 'lawless vision' in which Gabriel told him he was to visit God, and the text quotes the opening of the night-journey verse of the Qur'an (sura of the Children of Israel).
context: In Book IV, after an attack on Muhammad as the most impious man, the author lists Mehmed's fabrications; the Qur'an verse is cited to show the night-journey claim is false. The passage is therefore a critique of revelation claims, not of Ottoman policy.
limits: AUTHORSHIP DISPUTED (Maius; see works.json). The Qur'an quotation is the opening of 17:1 in the standard sense: the identification with Qur'an 17:1 is mine, from the words 'Praise to him who made his servant go by night', not stated by the source. The Greek is raw OCR with errors ('ϑεωρίαν' OK, 'ψῶλαι', 'IModus9', 'ἐπιδοσχέψοσθαι') and must be checked on the scan. No Latin was extracted for this passage (not verified).

ref: Chronicon maius, Liber III, cap. IV, c. Bekker p. 263 (CSHB 1838): during the 1453 siege, the Turkish sages of their 'religion and error' interpret a light over the city
quote_orig: καὶ αὐτὸ ἔκριναν οἱ τῆς μιαρᾶς αὐτῶν καὶ ἀσεβοῦς θρησκείας καὶ πλάνης σοφοὶ καὶ γραμματεῖς πῶς τὴν πόλιν κερδήσωσι τὸ φῶς ἐδήλου
own_translation_en: And the wise men and scribes of their impure and impious religion and error judged this, how they might win the city; the light made it clear. (Team translation of the raw OCR.)
licence_note: Bekker CSHB 1838 scan (archive.org): no licence field; PD by date (UNVERIFIED). Greek read from the OCR text layer only; not image-checked.
keys: τῆς μιαρᾶς αὐτῶν καὶ ἀσεβοῦς θρησκείας καὶ πλάνης
what_it_says: Phrantzes says that the Turkish learned men (wise men and scribes), whom he calls part of an impious religion and error, read a light seen over the city as a sign that they would take it.
context: During the 1453 siege the Turks saw a light over the city which they took as a sign; Phrantzes reports their interpretation as part of the siege narrative.
limits: The 'impious religion and error' is Phrantzes' judgement, given in a siege scene; it is not a doctrinal argument. Greek is raw OCR (line break after 'σο-' joined); not image-checked. Authorship of the Maius is disputed.

ref: Gennadios II, Confessio fidei posterior (homilia 'De Christianorum recta et vera fide' ad sapientes Agarenos), cap. I, Migne PG 160, col. 333-336 (approx.)

own_translation_en: We believe that there is one God who made all things, whatever exists anywhere, when they did not exist. He is neither body nor embodied, but lives in the act of understanding, and is the best, most perfect and wisest mind. (Team translation of the Latin.)
quote_latin: Credimus esse Deum qui omnia, quæcunque usquam sunt, cum non essent, ſecerit. Hic nec corpus est, nec corpore indutus, sed actu intelligendi vivit : et est mens optima, perfectissima et sapientissima.

ref: Gennadios (attributed), Confessio fidei I, 'Sermocinatio brevis et sapiens de nonnullis capitibus fidei nostrae ... cum amico Machumetis', Migne PG 160, col. 319-332 (approx.), first question of the Turk

own_translation_en: T. If there is one God, why do you also say there are three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? (Team translation of the Latin question of the Turkish interlocutor.)
quote_latin: T. Si itaque unus Deus est, cur dicitis etiam tres personas, Patrem videlicet, Filium et Spiritum Sanctum?
licence_note: Migne PG 160 (1866): public domain. Greek OCR unusable; Latin read from OCR layer, not image-checked.
what_it_says: In the dialogue the Turkish interlocutor objects to Christian Trinitarian doctrine as a contradiction with the oneness of God; the author answers that the Trinity is one God in three persons.
context: A question-and-answer dialogue between a Turk ('T.') and the patriarch ('P.'), printed in Migne with a Latin version. The Muslim objection to the Trinity is the only point of contact with Islam in the text I read.
